To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
readers' fixation times on ambiguous words are longer than on unambiguous words and that this effect is larger when the ambiguous word is equibiased than when it is non equibiased.

(i) reading times on the target word vary as a function of type of target word, type of ambiguous word and location of disambiguating information, (ii) reading times on later portions of the sentence vary as a function only of type of ambiguous word, and (iii) gaze durations on the target words vary as a function both of type of ambiguous and location of disambiguous information.
readers' eye movements are influenced by the frequency of ambiguous words, the frequency of the interpretations of ambiguous words, and the context in which ambiguous words appear.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of lexical ambiguity in the processing of sentences.
the processes of word identification and sentence comprehension.
the processes underlying the reading of ambiguous words.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of this study provide support for a model in which multiple meanings are activated in the course of lexical processing, but the degree of activation of these meanings is influenced by the frequency and prior context of the target word.

the eye-movement patterns of reading sentences containing lexically-ambiguous words depend on the nature of the ambiguity, the context of the ambiguity, and the location of disambiguating information.

the eye movement data from this study are consistent with a model of lexical ambiguity in reading in which multiple meanings are automatically activated, but the degree to which a particular meaning is activated depends on the relative frequencies of meanings in the lexicon, and on the degree to which the context supports one interpretation over the other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that lexical ambiguity can have a significant impact on eye movement patterns in reading.
the activation of multiple meanings for an ambiguous word is a normal process, but the activation of the correct meaning is influenced by the frequency and prior context of the word.

we have shown that lexical ambiguity resolution is a dynamic process, with multiple meanings of an ambiguous word being activated, and the degree of activation being determined by frequency and prior discourse context.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the activation of multiple meanings of an ambiguous word can occur even when the context strongly disfavors one of these meanings.
the activation of alternative meanings is not always the same, but depends on the nature of the ambiguity.
readers do not always fixate on the word they are reading, and that this is especially true for ambiguous words.
